CITY  OF  ALHAMBRA

  REGULARMEETING OF THE
  ALHAMBRA HOUSING AND COMMUNITY DEVELOPMENT
  CITIZEN ADVISORY COMMITTEE

The Regular Meeting of the Alhambra Housing and Community Development Citizen
Advisory (HCDA) Committee will be held on Tuesday, September 1, 2020, commencing
at 7:00 p.m. via teleconference and video conference.

  CORONAVIRUS (COVID-19) ADVISORY NOTICE

Consistent with Executive Orders No. N-29-20 and No. N-35-20 from the Executive
Department of the State of California and the County of Los Angeles Department of Public
Health Safer At Home Order, the Alhambra Housing and Community Development
Citizen Advisory Committee meeting will not be physically open to the public and the
meeting will take place via teleconference and video conference.

To watch and listen to the meeting: To maximize public safety while still maintaining
transparency and public access, members of the public can participate by using Zoom
Meeting as follows:

Zoom direct link:

https://us02web.zoom.us/j/84929673101?pwd=UjFJbVpqdmZKeGJKUzFMazZYNFYwZz0
9

Webinar ID: 849 2967 3101

Passcode: 806474

Or by telephone by dialing: 1-888-475-4499 (Toll Free) or 1-833-548-0276 (Toll Free) or
1-833-548-0282 (Toll Free) or 1-877-853-5257 (Toll Free)

Webinar ID: 849 2967 3101 and Passcode: 806474

Please Note: All members of the public calling or logging into the meeting will be muted
so that the meeting can proceed. For those wishing to speak on an agenda item, please
email Matthew Cuevas at mcuevas@cityofalhambra.org by 5:00 p.m. prior to the meeting
with the item number you wish to speak on and the phone number you will use when
calling or the name you will use when logging into the meeting. You should then call or
log into the meeting at least 5 minutes prior to its start time. Staff will unmute you and
announce you when it is your time to speak. You will have five minutes to speak, unless
that time is adjusted by the meeting Chair. Given the challenges of teleconference and
video conference meetings, all participants are encouraged to email their comments
prior to the beginning of the meeting.
 Comments can be emailed to the Matthew Cuevas at mcuevas@cityofalhambra.org by no
later than 5:00 p.m. on September 1, 2020 to ensure there is sufficient time to print the
emails prior to the beginning of the meeting. Comments will then be read into the record,
with a maximum allowance of 5 minutes per individual comment, subject to the Chair’s
discretion. If a comment is received after 5:00 p.m. but before the conclusion of the
meeting based upon its time stamp, the comment will still be included as a part of the
record of the meeting but will not be read into the record.

An agenda of the regular meeting is attached hereto incorporated herein by reference and
made a part hereof as though fully set forth herein.
   AGENDA
  REGULAR MEETING
HOUSING AND COMMUNITY DEVELOPMENT CITIZEN ADVISORY COMMITTEE
  TUESDAY, SEPTEMBER 1, 2020 AT 7:00 P.M.

1. ROLL CALL:
  Bill Vallejos, Chair  Mark Lee, Vice Chair
  Bonita Sharma-Ngan  Andrea Giese
  Marc Tousignant  Sasha Renée Pérez
  Maria Conchita Bañuelos  Yvette Cardenas
  Marcos Sayon

2. MINUTES
  None.

3. PROGRESS REPORTS
  Attached for the Committee’s review are copies of the Progress Reports for those programs
  utilizing Community Development Block Grant and HOME Funds. All figures indicate the
  progress made and services rendered to date for FY 2020-2021.
   Parks and Recreation - Case Management
   65 Case Management clients were served.
   0 Volunteer Hours of assistance were donated to the program.
   Community Development - Code Enforcement
   The Code Enforcement Division investigated a total of 47 complaints.
   16 were identified as confirmed complaints as stand-alone Health & Safety Issues.
   Code Enforcement staff referred 15 to the Housing Department programs.
   Community Development - Fair Housing
   The Housing Rights Center served approx. ____ clients.
   A variety of issues were discussed, including: evictions, security deposits, rent
  increases, repairs, contract questions, etc.
   Community Development - Housing Programs
   First-Time Home Buyer - HOME: 10 searching for a home, 0 escrow closed.
   HOME Major Rehabilitation: 2 in process, 0 completed.
   CDBG Minor Rehabilitation: 2 in process, 0 completed.

  Recommended Action
  Receive and file these informational reports.

4. 2019-2020 CONSOLIDATED ANNUAL PERFORMANCE AND EVALUATION
  REPORT (CAPER)
  Each year, the City of Alhambra is required by the Department of Housing and Urban
  Development to prepare a "Performance Report." This report covers the previous fiscal year's
  activities and expenditures. The report highlights the accomplishments of the year and the
  funds expended for each specific program.

  The CAPER provides for measurable performance against stated performance objectives.
  The City of Alhambra has been successful in meeting and in some cases exceeding its
   projected performance goals and objectives as defined in the Consolidated and Annual
  Action Plans.

  Staff will review this report with the committee. A copy of the full report will be available
  for public review and comment September 8 through September 23, 2020, and will be
  noticed in the Pasadena Star News, La Opinion, and World Journal. The report is due to
  HUD no later than January 6, 2021.

  Recommended Action
  Recommend approval to the City Council the Consolidated Annual Performance &
  Evaluation Report for 2019-2020.

5. COMMENTS FROM THE AUDIENCE
  Discussion from the public of any item not specified on the agenda. Comments must pertain
  to the business of the HCDA Citizen Advisory Committee. Public comments pertaining to
  the HCDA Committee’s business are welcome. Kindly limit all oral communications to five
  (5) minutes. Please complete the blue speaker card prior to the meeting and submit it to the
  Committee’s secretary.

6. COMMENTS AND CONCERNS FROM THE COMMITTEE
  Discussion from the Committee Members of any item(s) not specified on the agenda. Items
  discussed must pertain to the business of the HCDA Citizen Advisory Committee.

7. ADJOURNMENT

 Copies of the staff report or other written documentation relating to each item of business described herein
 above are on file in the office of Management Services, Alhambra City Hall, 111 S. First Street, Alhambra,
 CA, and are available for public inspection during regular office hours: 7:00 A.M. to 12:00 P.M., Monday
 through Thursday.
 Should any person have a question concerning any of the above agenda items prior to the meeting described
 herein, he or she may contact Mr. Matthew Cuevas, Management Analyst, either in person, at the
 Management Services Department located at City Hall, or call via telephone at (626) 570-5011, during
 regular business hours.

 Americans with Disabilities Act: If you require special assistance to participate in any City meeting, please
 contact the City Clerk's Office (626) 570-5090. Notification of at least 72 hours prior to the meeting will
 enable the City to make reasonable arrangements to ensure accessibility to this meeting.

 CR-05 - Goals and Outcomes
Progress the jurisdiction has made in carrying out its strategic plan and its action plan. 91.520(a)
This CAPER for FY 2019-2020 reviews the City’s specific achievements over the last year (July 1,
2019 through June 30, 2020) and an assessment of the progress in implementing the goals and
objectives of the five-year Consolidated Plan. This CAPER is the final year of implementing the FY
2015 – FY 2019 Consolidated Plan.
Goal 1: Provide Decent and Affordable Housing
  •  Priority 1: Affordable Housing - Housing Rehabilitation Program: During FY 2019-
  2020, one HOME-funded major rehabilitation project was completed and one project was
  underway. In addition, one CDBG-funded minor rehabilitation project was completed and
  one project was underway.
  •  Priority 2: First-Time Homebuyer Opportunities - First-Time Homebuyer Program
  (FTHB): During FY 2019-2020, two households closed escrow, nine approved households
  were searching for a home, and seven households were approved for assistance. In addition,
  the City received prequalification worksheets from 78 applicants.
  •  Priority 3: New Affordable Housing Construction/Opportunities - CHDO: As of July
  2020, the City has a cumulative CHDO disbursement/commitment ratio of about 23.7
  percent, exceeding the required 15 percent. In FY 2017-2018, HOME CHDO Reserve and
  Housing Asset Fund were used to rehabilitate and expand this property to a three-bedroom
  unit. The unit was completed in FY 2019.
  •  Priority 4: Code Enforcement Services - Code Enforcement: Overall, 929 code
  violations were investigated, of which 576 violations (62 percent) were located in low and
  moderate income areas. Code enforcement staff made 553 referrals to the Housing
  Rehabilitation Program, all were for properties in the low and moderate income areas.
  •  Priority 5: Equal Housing Opportunity - Fair Housing Services: In FY 2019-2020, the
  Housing Rights Center served 318 clients from Alhambra. Nearly all clients (88 percent)
  called for general housing services and about 12 percent required assistance with housing
  discrimination.
Goal 2: Provide Decent Living Environment through Neighborhood Improvements and
Community Services
  •  Priority 6: Community Facilities and Infrastructure - Capital Improvement Planning:
  The FY 2019-2020 Action Plan did not include any infrastructure improvement projects.
  The 2018 HUD Street Improvement Project benefitted approximately 950 people living in
  the low and moderate income area of Census Tract 480303 Block Group 1 (Olive Ave); 530
  of which were low and moderate income and 2,135 people living in the low and moderate
  income area of Census Tract 480304 Block Group 1 (Fifth Street); 1,415 of which were low
  and moderate (1,945 LMI persons total). In addition, the City completed six other public
  improvements projectsthat combined benefitted 228,040 low and moderate income persons.
  However, these accomplishments have previously been reported in the FY 2016 CAPER.

 Assess how the jurisdiction’s use of funds, particularly CDBG, addresses the priorities and specific
objectives identified in the plan, giving special attention to the highest priority activities identified.
The City of Alhambra was successful in implementing its Five-Year Consolidated Plan and Action
Plan for FY 2019-2020. CDBG funds were used to support the Minor Housing Rehabilitation
program, code enforcement, case management services, and fair housing services. HOME funds
were used in FY 2019-2020 to provide Major Housing Rehabilitation and First-Time Homebuyer
assistance. While the City did not meet the FY 2019-2020 rehabilitation goal, the City was able to
exceed the five-year goal of 35 households for the Consolidated Plan period.
Overall, the City met or exceeded all of its five-year goals with the exception of the development of
affordable units. Given the substantial costs of affordable housing development, the City completed
achieved two affordable units through acquisition/rehabilitation.

The City's Case Management program is a CDBG-funded activity qualified under Low and
Moderate Income Limited Clientele (LMC) and maintain demographic data on program
participants. The Case Management Program assisted a total of 105 persons. The participants are
split among three groups – Asians (41 persons), Hispanics (31 persons), Non-Hispanic Whites (27

The CDBG-funded Minor Housing Rehabilitation Program assisted one White Hispanic household
in FY 2019-2020. Two White Hispanic households and one Asian household were assisted with
HOME funds under First-Time Homebuyer and Major Rehabilitation programs.
While the Fair Housing services are funded under the CDBG Administration Cap (20 percent) and
not required to report demographic data, the Housing Rights Center also maintains statistics on its
clients. The Housing Rights Center assisted a total of 318 persons. Only 92 of these persons
assisted were included in Table 2 because the other persons assisted were classified as “others” race
or a race not listed in Table 2.
According to the Census Bureau 2018 estimates, 50.6 percent of Alhambra’s population is Asian,
37.8 percent is Hispanic, and 8.6 percent is White alone (not Hispanic or Latino). However, lower
income households tend to concentrate among minority households.

 Leveraging
Explain how federal funds leveraged additional resources (private, state and local funds), including
a description of how matching requirements were satisfied, as well as how any publicly owned land
or property located within the jurisdiction that were used to address the needs identified in the
plan.
The City of Alhambra has access to Federal and local resources to achieve its housing and
community development priorities. Specific funding sources will be utilized based on the
opportunities and constraints of each project or program.
The City received approval from the State to utilize its non-CDBG portion of the sales proceeds
($4,684,660) to fulfill its repayment obligation to the Housing Asset Fund (funds previously
borrowed by the City to pay the Supplemental Education Revenue Augmentation Fund (SERAF)).
As of July 2017, the Successor Agency had completely repaid the Housing Asset Fund. Overall, a
total of $5,019,279 is available in the Housing Asset Fund for affordable housing in the community.
The City utilized a portion of the Housing Asset Fund to acquire and rehabilitate 910 Benito
Avenue. The rehabilitation of 910 Benito Ave was completed in Fall 2019.
In addition, the City periodically pursues other state and federal grants for public improvement
projects.
HOME Match Requirements: The City is required to provide a 25 percent match on all HOME
Fund expenditures except for planning and administration, CHDO operating, CHDO capacity
building, and CHDO project-specific expenses when repayment is waived. The City has an excess
HOME match of over $5 million from previous years. This excess will be adequate to satisfy the
City’s HOME match requirements for an extended period of time.

Discuss the difference between goals and outcomes and problems encountered in meeting these

Describe the standards and procedures used to monitor activities carried out in furtherance of the

The City conducts monitoring reviews of all activities to ensure that programs are carried out in
accordance with the Consolidated Plan and Action Plan and in a timely manner. All programs and
projects are reviewed in February to determine if the program/project is moving forward in a
manner that will allow for the timely expenditure of the funds. On-site monitoring takes place
following the February review, and is conducted by the Management Analyst to ensure that statutory
and regulatory requirements are being met.
Monitoring Standards and Procedures: Internally, monitoring of the affordable housing program
is accomplished by City staff using current operating internal controls and management systems.
The controls are designed to ensure maintenance of complete and accurate program and financial
records, continuous tracking of program progress, separation of job duties, provision of periodic
reports, and public access to program documents. The City has established requirements for the
publishing and review of consultant/contractor RFPs and contracts, and requests for payment.
To ensure public review of the housing programs and to allow for public comments on goals and
progress, all new housing projects require hearings before the Planning Commission. All requests for
funding require a hearing before the City Council, and public input is received at the Housing and
Community Development Citizen Advisory (HCDA) Committee meetings. In addition, public
review meetings on CDBG-funded activities are held annually on proposed programs.
The City’s internal monitoring system is organized to maintain adequate records to ensure
compliance with State and Federal regulations regarding Nondiscrimination/Equal Opportunity,
Minimum Wage, Davis Bacon, Section 504/Handicapped Accessibility, Federal Housing Quality
Standards, and other mandated Federal Rules. The City will monitor its sub-recipient(s) on an annual
basis.
Intake Procedure for Housing Programs: All housing programs require that applicants complete
a pre-qualification form to determine that the applicant meets income requirements, is a legal citizen
or resident of the United States, and record household size and relationships. The First-Time
Homebuyer program also requires applicants be Alhambra residents for two consecutive years. If
the pre-qualification form is approved, the applicant must provide proof of household income, and
proof of household size of family to number of bedrooms.
For rehabilitation assistance, if the applicant receives preliminary approval that they meet the
program guidelines, City staff inspects the property to determine that the proposed rehabilitation
work is required, that the property meets City and State building codes, and tests for lead-based
paint on homes built prior to 1978.
Tracking System: The Director of Development Services and Development Services staff use a
rehabilitation board to track the progress of projects. This board provides a visual tracking system
for checking on projects completed, in progress, or on hold and indicates the staff member handling
the project.
Monitoring/Evaluation: Housing staff is responsible for monitoring all projects. However, the
Director of Development Services, or their designee, reviews the projects during different phases to
ensure rehabilitation works are eligible activities.

housing. These factors tend to disproportionately impact lower and moderate income households
due to their limited resources for absorbing the costs. These cost-burdened households require the
City’s special attention to address their underserved needs. Alhambra works to remove barriers to
affordable housing by implementing a Housing Element that is consistent with California law and
taking actions to reduce costs or provide off-setting financial incentives to assist in the production
of safe, high-quality, affordable housing. The City is committed to removing governmental
constraints that hinder the production of housing, and offers a “one-stop” streamlined permitting
process to facilitate efficient entitlement and building permit processing.
The City did not fund an affordable rental housing project during the reporting period. During FY
2019-2020, two households closed escrow, nine approved households were searching for a home,
and seven households were approved for assistance. In addition, the City received prequalification
worksheets from 78 applicants. Housing costs for the approved households meet Section 215
affordable housing requirements. However, given the high costs of ownership housing, approved
applicants have difficulty in finding an eligible home to purchase. The HCDA recommended
suspension of the FTHB program in FY 2020-2021.

  CAPER  22
OMB Control No: 2506-0117 (exp. 07/31/2015)
 The City purchased a single-family home at 910 Benito Avenue in 2017 using Housing Asset Fund
and was using HOME CHDO funds for the rehabilitation of this home. The contract for this
rehabilitation project was awarded to East LA Community Corporation in May 2017. Rehabilitation
was completed in Fall 2019.
The County of Los Angeles Community Development Commission Public Housing Authority
administers the Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher program on behalf of the City of
Alhambra. Currently, 564 Alhambra households are receiving Section 8 Vouchers as of August
2019.
The City does not identify targeted populations when providing affordable housing assistance. The
City’s affordable housing programs are made available to all persons and households provided the
household qualifies and does not exceed 80 percent of the median income criteria. Accessibility
improvements are eligible improvements under the City’s rehabilitation programs. Occasionally,
such improvements are included in the rehabilitation work scopes.
In addition to the CDBG- and HOME-funded affordable housing activities, the City fosters
affordable housing through the following:
  •  Implement the Housing Element and maintain compliance with State laws;
  •  Offer One-Stop streamlined permit processing for affordable and large-scale housing
  projects;
  •  Provide flexible development standards to promote high quality multi-family housing; and
  •  Offer a density bonus for affordable housing projects that meet State Density Bonus law.

OFFICIAL
  Minutes of the City of Alhambra’s
  HCDA Citizen Advisory Committee
  Special Meeting of September 1, 2020
  MEETING CONDUCTED VIA TELECONFERENCE/ZOOM DUE TO COVID-19.

  Chair Vallejos called the meeting to order at 7:06 p.m.

1. ROLL CALL:
  Committee Members Present:
  Bill Vallejos, Chair  Mark Lee, Vice Chair
  Maria Conchita Bañuelos  Marcos Sayon
  Marc Tousignant  Sasha Renée Pérez*

  *Committee Member Pérez joined the meeting at 7:25 p.m.

  Committee Members Absent:
  Andrea Giese
  Bonita Sharma-Ngan
  Yvette Cardenas

  City Staff Present:
  Lucy Garcia, Assistant City Manager
  Veronica Tam, Veronica Tam and Associates
  Matthew Cuevas, Management Analyst

2. MINUTES
  None.

3. PROGRESS REPORTS
  The Committee reviewed the reports. All figures indicate the progress made and services
  rendered to date for FY 2020-2021. Assistant City Manager Garcia gave an overview of the
  current progress reports, including the Parks and Recreation Case Management, and Code
  Enforcement. Assistant City Manager Garcia noted the Housing Rights Center provided their
  monthly report after the agenda packet had been complied and Management Analyst Cuevas
  would provide an update.

  Management Analyst Cuevas provided an overview of the Housing Rights Center’s report
  noting that 39 individuals from Alhambra sought assistance from the Housing Rights Center
  for the month of July.

  Assistant City Manager Garcia reminded the Committee that although the First Time Home
  Buyer program was not funded under the current year’s Action Plan, there were residual
  funds from prior years and there were 10 individuals searching for a home.

  Committee Action:
  By order of the Chair, the informational reports were received and filed.

4. 2019-2020 CONSOLIDATED ANNUAL PERFORMANCE AND EVALUATION
  REPORT (CAPER)
  Assistant City Manager Garcia gave an overview of what encompasses the Consolidated
  Page 1 of 6
 Annual Performance Evaluation Report (CAPER). She discussed the Goals and Outcomes
section of the CAPER in relation to all the City’s activities and the national objectives and
goals. Assistant City Manager Garcia also stated this CAPER reported on the last year of the
2015 – 2019 Consolidated Plan, and next year’s CAPER will cover year one of the City’s
recently adopted Consolidated Plan. Assistant City Manager Garcia reviewed the primary
accomplishments contained in the report:

  •  HOME Housing Minor Rehabilitation - 1 project underway.
  •  CDBG funded Minor Rehabilitation - 1 project underway.
  •  First Time Home Buyer - 2 households’ closed escrow, 9 households sought a home,
  and 7 households sought assistance.
  •  CHDO - in conjunction with support from the Housing Asset Fund, the City
  rehabilitated and expanded a 3-bedfroom property unit in 2019 utilizing both CHDO
  and First Time Home Buyer program.
  •  Code Enforcement – 929 violations were investigated and 576 were located in the
  low-moderate areas as required by CDBG program guidelines. Additionally, 553
  referrals were made to the housing rehabilitation program/Housing Rights Center.
  Assistant City Manager Garcia reminded the Committee that Code Enforcement had
  changed the way statistics were compiled for the new Consolidated Plan and 500
  violations in the target area is the now the target goal and will monitored moving
  forward.

Assistant City Manager Garcia then discussed the equal housing opportunity program under
fair housing services and any HUD funded capital improvement efforts during the program
year and noted:

  •  Fair Housing Services – 318 clients were served in Alhambra. Of those clients, 4
  percent required assistance with housing discrimination and the remainder required
  general housing services.

  •  Capital Improvement Program – prior year project regarding street rehabilitation
  program that was spent in 2019 and benefited 950 individuals who lived in that
  project’s particular low-moderate area census tract. In addition, 6 other public
  improvements were also combined to provide a public benefit to other low-moderate
  income areas.

Assistant City Manager Garcia then reviewed the Case Management Program, Housing, and
Administration efforts that included:

  •  Case Management – 105 new clients, 439 reassurance calls made, and 4,000 meals
  were served in the 2019 year
  •  Commercial Rehabilitation – no major economic development activities, as it was
  deemed a low priority need during the development of the Consolidated Plan.
  •  Planning and Administration – staff time to monitor and implement CDBG and
  HOME programs.

Assistant City Manager Garcia then briefly discussed a section of the report that outlines the
different activities funded by CDBG and HOME and the categories and goals they fulfill.
She noted the majority of the City’s goals were met with the exception of homeowner
housing rehabilitation program, which came in at 33 percent served. Assistant City Manager
  Page 2 of 6
 Garcia stated that although the number appeared low, she stated the City given the nuances of
this year, it is expected the activity will improve by the end of 2021. She stated the report
currently does not contain the amount expended during the program year since the City is
still going through the accruals between the 19-20 fiscal year, but they will be completed in
time to present to City Council and send to HUD.

Assistant City Manager Garcia touched on other needs outlined in the CAPER relating to
homelessness and the City has contracted with a new provider, LACADA, to assume
navigation, case management work and crisis sheltering referrals and will apply to the new
fiscal year and Consolidated plan. She noted these new services are not being funded through
CDBG funds but through the Housing Successor Asset fund and other grant funding sources.

Veronica Tam, Veronica Tam and Associates, clarified public improvement projects are
really 6 major locations throughout the City under one larger, umbrella project. She also
stated in this year’s CAPER, activities under the CDBG COVID funds, such as COVID-19
testing, senior meals and emergency housing assistance would be included (statuses). Ms.
Tam further stated the findings to the Analysis of Impediments to Fair Housing Choice
would also be incorporated into this year’s CAPER since it was prepared during the 2019
fiscal year.

Assistant City Manager Garcia concluded her presentation by noting that the CAPER is
typically submitted in September; however, HUD has extended the submission deadline to
January 2021; nonetheless, the City has elected to proceed with a September submittal.

Committee Member Tousignant inquired about a table on page 3 of the CAPER regarding the
public services number and how it was exceeding the target by such a large percent.

Ms. Tam responded it is due to a glitch in the HUD reporting system, and each time an
activity is added, the system duplicates the counts of individuals that will be served.

Committee Member Tousignant asked about the CDBG funds that came due to the
coronavirus and how close the City was to meeting the target number of assisting 200
households.

Assistant City Manager Garcia responded the City exceeded the 200 and is now utilizing the
additional funds that were provided through the State from the CARES Act.

Committee Member Tousignant asked if it would be possible to schedule a presentation from
the mental health clinician and their experience on working on homelessness in the City.

Assistant City Manager Garcia clarified that the City does not fund that particular position
but is done in partnership with LA County Department of Mental Health.

Committee Member Tousignant motioned for a presentation at a future meeting on the City’s
efforts on homelessness specifically street outreach with the police department.

Committee Action:
Committee Member Tousignant moved, seconded by Committee Member Pérez.
Ayes:  Vallejos, Lee, Sayon, Bañuelos, Tousignant and Pérez.
Noes:  None.
Abstain: None.
  Page 3 of 6
   Committee Member Tousignant asked about the leveraging section and the successor funds,
  and the need to be more expansive on the Measure H and COG funds as opposed to just that
  one source.

  Ms. Tam responded she could expand upon that and make it clearer the City receives
  additional funds as result of Measure H and the COG for homelessness, and the State
  CARES Act for emergency housing assistance and other COVID response. She stated she
  would revise those number before the final report is sent to the City Council.

  Committee Member Tousignant indicated he felt it would be a good thing to expand upon
  and would be a good local story for the City Council to see as well as HUD.

  Committee Action:
  Committee Member Bañuelos moved to approve the 2019 – 2020 Consolidated Annual
  Performance Evaluation Report to City Council with the requested changes, seconded by
  Committee Member Lee.
  Ayes:  Vallejos, Lee, Sayon, Bañuelos, Tousignant and Pérez.
  Noes:  None.
  Abstain: None.

5. COMMENTS FROM THE AUDIENCE

  Management Analyst Cuevas read an email comment received from resident Ms. Meehar
  Tom regarding if CDBG funds could be used to save six historic homes.

6. COMMENTS AND CONCERNS FROM THE COMMITTEE

  Committee Member Pérez asked about the comments the resident submitted and if that could
  be discussed at a future meeting to see if its possible, and if not, where would it be
  appropriate to address her concerns.

  Committee Member Bañuelos inquired about the homes that were mentioned during the
  comments from the audience period, if they were officially marked as historical or if that was
  her opinion and felt the resident should start with the historical society.

  Assistant City Manager Garcia responded she would need to consult with the Community
  Development Department in regards to the history of those homes, and do additional research
  if CDBG funds could be made available for that purpose and staff could follow up at a later
  time.

  Committee Member Pérez stated the Planning Commission recently discussed if these homes
  were historic and some paperwork was found, but was unsure what would qualify and if the
  paperwork that was found would justify that.

  Vice Chair Lee inquired if this item could be placed on next meeting’s agenda.

  Assistant City Manager Garcia answered she would need to do additional research on this
  item but it could be brought back at a later time.

  Page 4 of 6
 Committee Member Bañuelos asked if an acknowledgement for receiving the comment and
that it is being looked into could be provided to the resident.

Assistant City Manager Garcia answered yes.

Vice Chair Lee commented on the Chair doing a good job, but for the next meeting and the
need to adhere to official format, for example when presentations are done and then
Committee Members can make comments or ask their questions after in order keep the
meetings short, instead of recent meetings where Committee Members ask questions in the
middle of presentations, and causes the meetings to go on and on and wanted to get
Committee Member thoughts.

Committee Member Bañuelos commented the Committee should follow Robert’s Rules of
Order depending on what the discussion is.

Vice Chair Lee responded that Robert’s Rules states the presentation or any comments,
Committee Members could wait until its done then the Committee Members can ask their
questions or make their comments. He stated he would really like to follow that guideline,
and City staff recommendation, and doesn’t want to spend three hours at a meeting, but a
comfortable time where issues can be debated and discussed so the Committee can help the
citizens of Alhambra.

Committee Member Bañuelos stated it helps when the Chair runs the meetings because it
pushes it along, and mentioned the last meeting the Chair was not present the meeting ran
very long. She agreed with Vice Chair Lee, out of respect to the other Committee Members,
it’s important to follow the procedures.

Vice Chair Lee also commented if City staff could help regulate the meetings as well and
make sure the meetings are adhering to the rules and regulations.

Committee Member Pérez indicated she was fine with conducting future meetings either way
whether it is following Robert’s Rules or waiting until after presentations or PowerPoints are
given and was open to what the rest of Committee would like to do.

Committee Member Sayon commented that the Chair has done a good job in prior meetings
by making sure they make progress, and any questions that were off topic, the Chair could
direct the Committee back to stay on topic. He noted the meetings are pretty efficient when
the Chair runs them. Committee Member Sayon felt it wasn’t too big of a concern to him
because the Chair does a good job of keeping the Committee on topic, and is ok with how he
runs the meetings.

(Chair Vallejos experienced technical issues with hearing the Committee Members so
Assistant City Manager Garcia indicated Vice Chair Lee could take over the remainder of the
meeting.)

Vice Chair Lee asked for a motion for adjournment.

Committee Member Pérez motioned to adjourn the meeting, Committee Member Tousignant
seconded the motion.

Committee Action:
  Page 5 of 6
   Ayes:  Vallejos, Lee, Sayon, Bañuelos, Tousignant and Pérez.
  Noes:  None.
  Abstain:  None.

7. ADJOURNMENT

  Meeting adjourned at 7:50 p.m.
